title: His tune Loner/Number Nine and the Sampson dispute
summary: He says he wrote a tune in Cuba, had Edgar Sampson arrange it, and feels Stompin' at the Savoy and Goodman borrowed it.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: When did you first record with Ella Fitzgerald?

That band recorded, the first recording Ella made with that band, I think, was in '33. In fact, they recorded Number Nine that I wrote. I wrote that tune in Cuba. And I heard it all along. When I came here with the tune, one day I said to Edgar Sampson, Edgar, I got a tune that I wrote in Cuba in '28 and '29. I never done nothing with it. And I would like for you to make an arrangement for the band. So he says, great.
My -- the name of the tune was Loner. And the first brass tune with two melodies going. And the number go pah, pah, doo-doo-doo-dee-doo-dee-doo-dee-doo, pah,
puh, pee, doo-dee-doo-dee-doo, pah, puh. So he made an arrangement. We started playing that song.

Before I know, Sampson came with a number called Stumping the Savoy, the same idea. Benny Goodman take the song and made a hit, and the drum beat, the way, the same idea in my song. I've got so many -- every one singles.

And then Teddy Wilson start hauling me. He want me to give my tune to Goodman. I said no. I write that tune to die, and I don't want nobody make no money on my music notes. I'm already hurt, because Sampson, he took my tune. And now he wrote identical thing, changed a not, but the idea, no (inaudible) tune been written before, two things going on like that.

Like I say, one, dah, dah, bah-dum-pah-dee-dee-deeo-dah, dah, dah. That was -- I brought that from Cuba. I wrote it in Cuba in 1929. I still got the receipt from the Vocalion -- we call it the Vocalion, the license for that recording --
-- what I never got a nickel for. But I let it die there. So we keeping going, keeping going, and Duke wanted me to go with the band.
